claims.text: Australia's Psychology Board of Australia (via Ahpra) states that registered psychologists using AI must still meet existing code-of-conduct obligations — accountability, understanding the tool, transparency of its use, informed consent, and ethical/legal compliance — so AI does not create a new exemption from professional duties.

sources.title: Applying your code of conduct to evolving technologies
sources.whatItMeasured: Guidance note to all registered health practitioners (including psychologists) on the principles to apply when using or integrating AI into practice, translating existing code-of-conduct obligations.

claims.scope: Registered psychologists in Australia (Ahpra National Scheme).

claims.quote: Ahpra and the National Boards have developed principles for practitioners to consider when using or looking to integrate AI into their practice.

claims.text: Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) concluded that the standing exclusion for 'digital mental health tools' from medical-device regulation is no longer appropriate and requires urgent review, and signalled that AI scribes that propose diagnosis/treatment may meet the definition of a medical device requiring pre-market approval.

sources.title: Clarifying and strengthening the regulation of Medical Device Software including Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Outcomes Report
sources.whatItMeasured: Outcome of a 2024 TGA review (consultation Sep–Oct 2024; 53 formal responses, 600+ stakeholders) of whether existing medical-device software/AI legislation is fit for purpose, including findings on digital scribes and digital mental health tools.

claims.scope: Australian regulatory framework for software/AI as a medical device, including tools used by registered psychologists (digital mental health tools, AI scribes).
claims.refuteNotes: Source real (TGA consultation/outcomes page; report published 30 July 2025 per TGA and corroborating legal/medical trade coverage). Binds Australian supply of mental-health AI; psychology-relevant via Finding 8 (digital mental health tools). Within window.
claims.quote: The digital mental health tools exclusion is no longer appropriate and urgent review is needed.

claims.text: The Australian Psychological Society's Professional practice guidelines for the use of AI and emerging technologies (released after the PsyBA Code of Conduct took effect on 1 Dec 2025) state that AI must not substitute for professional decision-making or clinical judgement and that psychologists remain fully responsible for all aspects of service delivery, including AI-generated outputs, requiring tool-specific written informed consent.

sources.title: Using AI in psychological practice: How the new APS practice guidelines help psychologists
sources.whatItMeasured: Explanation of the APS Professional practice guidelines for the use of AI and emerging technologies (member resource) covering clinical accountability, evidence-based standards, specific informed consent, data security, bias vigilance and digital literacy for psychologists.

claims.scope: Australian psychologists who are APS members (peak body representing ~25,000 members), operating under the Psychology Board of Australia Code of Conduct effective 1 Dec 2025.
claims.refuteNotes: Source real (APS insights page, last reviewed Feb 2026; guidelines released late 2025/early 2026 alongside PsyBA Code of Conduct effective 1 Dec 2025). Applies to Australian psychologist population. Within window. Member-only guideline, but described publicly by APS.
claims.quote: psychologists remain fully responsible for all aspects of service delivery, including any outputs generated by technology.

claims.text: A peer-reviewed validation study of an LLM-powered conversational depression-screening tool (embedding the Beck Depression Inventory Fast Screen into a ChatGPT-4o dialogue) found the automated scores correlated strongly with clinician BDI-FS ratings (Spearman rho ≈ 0.79) among adults seeking psychological consultation, suggesting AI can complement — not replace — clinical judgement in psychological assessment.

sources.title: Evaluating the Efficacy of AI-Based Interactive Assessments Using Large Language Models for Depression Screening: Development and Usability Study
sources.whatItMeasured: 164 attendees (≥18 yrs) at the Psychological Crisis Early Warning and Monitoring Technology Research Center, Zhengzhou Normal University, China, sequentially screened Jul 2024–Jan 2025; 28 with depression and 87 without completed the LLM-based Automated Assessment Paradigm, scored against clinician diagnosis.

claims.scope: Adults seeking psychological consultation in an urban Chinese university-affiliated centre (not an Australian sample); generalisable to psychologist-delivered assessment only with caution.
claims.refuteNotes: Source real (PubMed PMID 41529832; JMIR Form Res 2026;10:e78401, published 13 Jan 2026; full text via doi.org). Peer-reviewed. claims.quote: The AAP framework combines the interactivity and personalization of NLP-powered tools with the psychometric rigor of traditional scales.

sources.title: Examining the role of AI technology in online mental healthcare: opportunities, challenges, and implications, a mixed-methods review
sources.whatItMeasured: PRISMA systematic review of 29 peer-reviewed RCTs/observational/case studies (MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, EMBASE, Cochrane) on AI applications in online mental healthcare, with meta- and network meta-analysis of pre/post intervention outcomes.

claims.scope: Global body of AI online mental-health intervention studies (US/Canada context cited); not specific to Australia.
claims.refuteNotes: Source real (Front. Psychiatry 15:1356773, published 7 May 2024; doi 10.3389/fpsyt.2024.1356773). Peer-reviewed, PRISMA-registered. Population is the literature, not a single national cohort; scope stated. Within window (2024).
claims.quote: AI-delivered self-guided interventions demonstrated medium to large effects on managing mental health symptoms, with dropout rates comparable to non-AI interventions.
